title: 2025-12-09-poc-burst-capacity-fallbacks-sync
summary: Weekly POC sync to review last 48h throughput tests. Redwood presented tuned continuous-batching + concurrency profiles; customer reported intermittent queuing under bursty traffic. Agreement to run a 4-hour burst test at 2x load with KV-cache enabled and to validate fallback policy behavior. Redwood to provide log bundle and a short runbook for diagnosing queue backpressure. Next meeting set after benchmark window.
next_steps: Redwood to share raw perf logs and config snapshot (Marcus)
Maple to run 4-hour burst replay at 2x peak on staging and share traces (Liam)
Schedule SE deep-dive for kernel/quantization behavior if tail P99 high (tentative: week of 12/15)
Redwood to send updated cost estimate for dedicated pool with burst buffer enabled
action_items: Marcus Lee | export perf logs + config snapshot | 2025-12-11
Liam O'Connor | run 4h 2x-burst replay on staging and send traces | 2025-12-12
Avery Chen | provide updated pricing and sample piloting contract | 2025-12-13
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Sofia Ruiz (CSM), Priya Nair (Maple Eng Manager), Liam O'Connor (Maple SRE), Tess Hammond (Maple CTO), Samir Rao (ML Eng), Jules Park (Product)

Summary (auto): review of throughput runs, queueing under burst, config tuning, next steps and log handoff.

[00:00] Avery (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — good to see the Maple team. Quick check, audio okay?
[00:09] Priya: yep, audio good here.
[00:12] Marcus (SE): I'll share my screen in a sec, I'm going to walk through the 48-hour run results and then we can zoom into the weird tail behavior Liam flagged.
[00:22] Liam: cool, thanks. We saw a couple of 500-ish spikes and then a growing queue — not sure if that's on your side or our client replay tool.
[00:30] Marcus: right, we'll go through request traces. Quick reminder of config used: continuous batching enabled, target concurrency 6 per model worker, batch size cap 128 tokens, kv-cache off for the first run, quantization at 4-bit AQT.
[00:44] Marcus: sharing slide deck now — link in chat: https://redwood.app/s/poc/maple/12-09-run1
[00:50] [00:56] Slide: throughput and latency summary
[00:56] Marcus: overall sustained throughput averaged 340 reqs/s for the 10-minute rolling windows, cost about $0.018 per 1k tokens with our current pooling. But when we injected a burst at t+30m the queue depth climbed for ~90s and we saw tail P99s jump from 120ms to 2.6s.
[01:15] Priya: ok that's the spike — it's enough to impact our customer SLAs. We need to understand whether that's because of our client pattern (very spiky) or because the batching/concurrency knobs aren't right for this workload.
[01:27] Marcus: preliminary hypothesis: continuous batching settings were optimized for steady-state throughput. With highly bursty arrivals, the batcher waits for the batch-window to fill or for concurrency to free up, which increases latency. We can tune solver rules — two levers: reduce batch wait (aggressively flush) or increase concurrency and rely on autoscaling/burst buffer.
[01:45] Tess: question — you mentioned burst buffer, did you mean Redwood's dedicated burst capacity? How does that behave with fallbacks to hosted variants?
[01:53] Avery: yeah, good question. We exposed a burst policy in the Dedicated plan — if the pool is saturated it will route to warm standbys or a lower-cost hosted variant. The fallback has configurable SLO thresholds and we can set hard caps to avoid unpredictable cost. Note: the fallback path may change model variant or quantization which can affect output quality slightly.
[02:12] Samir: does fallback preserve KV cache / context for the same session? We need stateful sessions for chat use-cases.
[02:19] Marcus: good call — not by default. Fallback to another pool will not have the same warm KV cache; that's why we recommend prefix-caching on the client or sticky routing for conversation sessions. For the POC we can test sticky routing behavior.
[02:33] [02:40] Marcus: let me show the timeline traces from the injection run — here's the waterfall view (note transcription may misname some fields): request ID x1a2 — you can see 7 concurrent inflight at t+30, the batcher built a 64-token batch, waited ~120ms for the flush timer, then executed. Meanwhile queue backlog reached 48 requests.
[03:05] Liam: hmm we are seeing backlog on our side tool as well but our generator shows burst at 1.8x not 2x, so that might explain partial mismatch. I can re-run with canonical replay.
[03:15] Marcus: yeah let's isolate. We added a quick mitigation in run2: kv-cache enabled and concurrency bumped to 10, with batch wait set to 30ms. Results: average throughput up to 420 rps, P95 slightly improved, tail P99 dropped to 780ms but still above your SLA.
[03:35] Priya: 780ms is better but still scary for synchronous UX path. What happened in the 780ms cases — were they all the same requests?
[03:42] Marcus: looking at traces, many of those are large-token requests (~1.2k tokens) that got batched late. Also clock jitter and kernel-switch delays on the GPU instance coincided with a background housekeeping job — we flagged that as an anomaly in the first run.
[03:58] Jules: any suspicion about instance sizing? We are testing on g5-style equivalent; would a higher memory or v100 alternative change behavior?
[04:06] Marcus: instance flavor matters mainly for throughput and context window. The bigger difference for tail is scheduling: more workers with smaller concurrency each reduces head-of-line blocking. So we can either increase concurrency per worker or spin additional workers for the dedicated pool. That's a tradeoff vs cost.
[04:23] [04:30] Avery: quick interjection — we've seen teams avoid high P99 by combining three things: 1) lower batch wait, 2) sticky routing + prefix cache for chat sessions, and 3) burst buffer with soft-fallback to a slightly quantized hosted variant. All together maintain UX and cap cost exposure.
[04:46] Tess: but sticky routing means hot pins to nodes, could that reduce effective pooling and kill cost-efficiency?
[04:53] Marcus: yes, there's a cost tradeoff. For Maple's use-case we recommend hybrid: sticky for a short tail of active sessions (15-30s), then release. That keeps reuse high while minimizing long-lived pins.
[05:06] Samir: curious on quantization QA — you said fallback might change quantization, do we have eval diffs? We care about hallucination rates.
[05:13] Marcus: we ran a quick eval set: 4-bit quantized variant had negligible degradation on 9/10 conversational prompts but a couple of long form generation tests had slight tokenization noise. We'll share the eval spreadsheet: https://redwood.app/refs/quant-eval-maple.csv
[05:28] [05:36] Marcus: demoing the queue dashboard now — showing inflight, queue depth, avg batch size over time. See the spike at t+30. We can set an alert to fire when queue depth > 30 for >20s and auto-increase concurrency or trigger fallback.
[05:54] Liam: that alert would be useful. Also want to capture kernel-level metrics so we can correlate with our infra traces — can you include per-instance GPU util and kernel-mode switches in the logs?
[06:05] Marcus: yes we'll include the per-instance metrics in the bundle. Note: the raw logs are large — we'll provide a filtered tarball and a pointer to the S3 bucket for full data.
[06:16] Priya: one operational question: when the fallback hits hosted variant, how do you surface the change to app layer? We prefer an in-band header or status that allows us to measure fidelity differences.
[06:26] Avery: good call — we can surface a header X-Redwood-Fallback: variant=hosted-v2, quant=4bit in the response metadata, or alternatively send an event to your tracing system. We'll add both options.
[06:41] [06:50] Marcus: moving on to concrete tuning suggestions we tested in run3: 1) reduce batch wait to 20ms, 2) concurrency 12, 3) enable KV prefix caching, 4) bump worker pool to 6 (from 4). This improved latency but increased cost ~14% on our cost model.
[07:10] Priya: can you quantify cost per 1M tokens under that setting vs the baseline? We need to show finance.
[07:16] Avery: baseline estimate was $18 per 1M tokens; tuned setting around $20.5 per 1M tokens. We'll include a cost delta spreadsheet.
[07:25] Samir: one more thing — for the chat users who have long histories, prefix caching seems critical. Do you have a recommended TTL for caches?
[07:32] Marcus: we typically recommend TTL of 300s for active conversations, with a soft eviction after 1k unique sessions. That keeps hit rates high during bursts.
[07:40] [07:48] Priya: ok, what about a fail-open vs fail-closed policy — do you allow forcing fail-open to hosted so that requests never fail, or fail-closed to maintain strict data residency?
[07:58] Avery: both options exist. For customers with data residency constraints we support fail-closed and surface a 429 to the client. For those prioritizing availability, fail-open to a vetted hosted region (with contract PII handling) is possible. We'll need to document the legal protections.
[08:14] Tess: legal will want the details; put that in the security doc.
[08:18] Sofia (CSM): noted, I'll attach the SOC2/ISO excerpt and the failover table.
[08:23] [08:30] Marcus: digging back into the runs — here's a short run correlation that shows the queue continued to grow because the batcher flush timer was hit before concurrency freed up. Small change: aggressive flush on small batches reduced P99 for small requests, but for large requests it didn't help. So we recommend differentiated policies by token-length class.
[08:50] Samir: interesting — so token-length aware batching. Is that already supported or would that be a feature request?
[08:57] Marcus: it's supported in our tuning layer as an experimental policy; for production we can enable it per pool. It's called "adaptive length bucketing" in the config. We'll enable in a canary run.
[09:08] [09:15] Priya: can we walk through the planned 4-hour burst test? What exactly will Redwood measure and what do you need from us?
[09:22] Marcus: plan: Redwood will run a controlled replay script against your staging endpoint using the same trace as your production peak but at 2x intensity for 4 hours. We'll capture request traces, batcher metrics, queue depths, per-instance GPU metrics, and fallback events. From Maple we need canonical replay payloads and a staging endpoint that matches network characteristics. Also we need the SRE to collect their side traces.
[09:45] Liam: I can prepare the canonical replay. We'll run it Wednesday morning PST — can you reserve the pool and set the config snapshot?
[09:53] Avery: yes we'll stand up a dedicated ephemeral pool with burst buffer enabled for that window. We'll also tag all fallback events with your crm id MAP-2025-0983.
[10:03] Marcus: two operational notes: 1) we'll start with kv-cache on for warmed sessions; 2) we'll instrument an experiment toggle to hard-force fallback for 30s at t+90 to verify sticky routing behavior.
[10:18] [10:24] Priya: sounds good. For the experiment toggle, will that destroy sticky session state? We want to see how many sessions lose KV cache.
[10:31] Marcus: the toggle will route new requests to fallback; sticky sessions currently only maintain on a per-worker basis, so yes some sessions will be redirected and lose cache — that's expected and part of the test. We'll correlate with session IDs and report hit rates.
[10:46] Tess: on metrics and dashboards, can you export a Grafana dashboard JSON so we can import directly?
[10:52] Marcus: yes we'll share the dashboard JSON and the alert rules. Link: https://redwood.app/dash/maple/burst-dashboard.json
[10:58] [11:09] Conversation drift — brief side chat about holidays and team locations, slight crosstalk.
[11:20] Marcus: quick note — we noticed a small set of requests where our kernel selection favored a fallback CPU path due to memory pressure on a particular node. That node had a background snapshot job. We'll add node-level QoS guards to prevent snapshot jobs from scheduling during critical windows.
[11:37] Liam: please include the node ID in the log bundle so we can coordinate with our infra team.
[11:41] Marcus: will do.
[11:44] [11:51] Priya: one more question on SSO/permissions — our security team wants to ensure only SREs can trigger failover tests. Can you add role gating?
[11:58] Avery: yes, role-based gating is supported via RBAC in the console; we'll create a policy template and share.
[12:05] Samir: any concerns about model fidelity when fallback hits hosted variant? We need to measure hallucinations and rouge-type metrics.
[12:12] Marcus: we'll run the eval set both on your dedicated pool and on the hosted fallback and provide a diff report. Expect tiny diffs on conversational QA, higher diffs on long creative generation.
[12:25] [12:31] Marcus: ok, action item recap: Redwood will push logs and config snapshot by 12/11, Maple will run 4h replay by 12/12, Redwood to stand up ephemeral pool and share dashboard + alert rules, and we'll reconvene after the replay.
[12:47] Avery: let's try to keep the next meeting to 30 minutes focused on result validation. Tentatively schedule for 12/13 or 12/15 depending on replay completion.
[12:58] Priya: 12/15 works for us; we'll confirm internally.
[13:04] [13:12] Sofia (CSM): I'll follow up with the SOC2 excerpt and the failover table; also adding the security contact point.
[13:20] Marcus: any last questions?
[13:24] Tess: none here, thanks team.
[13:26] Avery: thanks everyone, circling back with the links and logs.
[13:31] Meeting end.
